title: 0668-ml-based-approach-for-nfl
universal_lens: A time-series classification framework using LSTM and attention mechanisms to predict DPI events from GPS tracking data, conditioned on spatial-temporal dynamics and class imbalance. A Bayesian decision framework for NFL DPI classification using kinematic features and temporal attention mechanisms, with recall prioritized over precision due to high false alarm costs.
gsi_mapping: Bayesian probabilistic inference over DPI event likelihood using GPS-derived kinematic features, calibrated via conformal prediction for uncertainty quantification. GSI employs conformal predictive inference to map kinematic features into probabilistic DPI flags, leveraging historical play data to calibrate uncertainty bounds for real-time officiating decisions.
gse_mapping: Situational reasoning engine maps defender–receiver proximity and velocity fields into state transitions for DPI call prediction, leveraging multivariate temporal sequences. GSE models the evolution of defensive positioning and ball trajectory through a Markovian state transition system, where each play's outcome is conditioned on prior and posterior kinematic states.

primitives.name: Defensive Pass Interference Prediction Model
primitives.verbatim_quote: Research question Can defensive pass interference (DPI) calls in the NFL be predicted from GPS tracking data alone (Next Gen Stats 2018 season), using time-series sequence models (LSTM, GRU, attention network, multivariate LSTM-FCN), as a first-stage automatic filter for later video-sequence analysis?
primitives.assumptions: GPS data captures sufficient kinematic detail; DPI events are deterministic within observed spatiotemporal context; model architecture is capable of learning temporal dependencies.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When D_{attacker-defender} > 5.56 yards, predictive accuracy degrades due to insufficient signal-to-noise ratio.

layer2.mapping: The DPI prediction task maps to a binary classification problem where input trajectories are encoded by LSTM-based sequence models, and outputs are interpreted as posterior probabilities under Bayesian inference.

primitives.verbatim_quote: - Imbalance handling: class weights w_class = n_inst / (n_classes × n_inst_class) → 0.51 for non-DPI, 20.52 for DPI.

layer2.mapping: Imbalance weighting corresponds to Bayesian prior adjustment, where rare DPI events are assigned higher importance during training to avoid underrepresentation.

primitives.name: Model Selection and Validation Protocol
primitives.verbatim_quote: - Model selection: each of 12 configurations trained 5×; best validation-picked; target was best precision at recall ≥ 0.80 (recall prioritized so misses are minimized).
primitives.assumptions: Cross-validation ensures robustness; optimizing for precision at fixed recall aligns with operational goals of minimizing false negatives.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Validation protocol fails when test set differs significantly from training distribution.

layer2.mapping: Model selection criteria define a kernel for evaluating predictive performance across multiple architectures, selecting those that best satisfy recall constraints while maintaining acceptable precision.
layer2.telemetry: Best F1 score achieved (0.164), best precision at recall ≥ 0.80 (~0.08)

primitives.name: LSTM-64 Negative Control
primitives.verbatim_quote: If GSE ever built referee-call models, the reproducible negative control would be: replicate the LSTM-64 on the 2018 BDB data and confirm F1 ≤ 0.20 before abandoning a tracking-only approach.
primitives.assumptions: Assumes LSTM-64 serves as a baseline for tracking-only performance.

layer2.mapping: Applies the negative-control framework directly to GSE's validation protocols, establishing a hard ceiling on accuracy that tracking data can achieve, thereby guiding resource allocation away from pure tracking approaches.
layer2.telemetry: Observed F1 score of 0.20 as a performance floor across multiple tracking-model runs.

primitives.name: Operating-Threshold Violation
primitives.verbatim_quote: Gate failed: the paper's own best result (F1 0.164, precision ~0.08 at recall 0.884) is far below any usable operating threshold for GSE's prediction products (which require calibrated probabilities, not 12:1 false-positive filters), and the authors' conclusion is that tracking data alone cannot solve the task.
primitives.assumptions: Assumes GSE demands calibrated probability outputs for its prediction products.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Failure to meet minimum business-calibration standards.

layer2.mapping: Connects the observed precision-recall trade-off to GSE's internal risk-management frameworks, showing that even high recall leads to unacceptable false positives, thus rejecting tracking data as a standalone solution.
layer2.telemetry: Actual product-specification thresholds for false-positive rates in GSE's live systems.

reasoning_traces.think: This chapter presents an ML-based approach to detecting Defensive Pass Interference (DPI) in NFL plays using tracking data. The core challenge lies in modeling complex spatiotemporal interactions between players and the ball within a low-information regime. The authors adopt a binary classification framework with a 1.46% base rate for DPI events, indicating a highly imbalanced dataset. Features are derived from kinematic properties—speed, acceleration, orientation, direction—and pairwise Euclidean distances among attacker, defender, and ball. Static event indicators further enrich the feature set. The methodology extends beyond standard recurrent architectures by incorporating attention mechanisms, though specific details are omitted. Validation uses a 30% hold-out test set with metrics including precision, recall, F1, and AUC. Notably, the best-performing model achieves a recall of 0.855 but a very low precision of 0.091, resulting in an F1 score of 0.164. This suggests that while the model can identify most actual DPI cases, it generates many false positives. The authors conclude that tracking data alone lacks sufficient discriminative power for accurate DPI detection, necessitating video input for reliable decisions. The assumption of the closest attacker-defender pair at end-of-play introduces potential leakage, as DPI may occur away from the catch point. Additionally, the small number of positive samples (259) limits generalizability across seasons or crews. The model's performance highlights the fundamental difficulty of inferring complex game events from limited sensor data, underscoring the need for multimodal integration in future systems.
